title: Stream multiplexing SDK design and tooling PRD (WIP)
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working PRD for a new Hosted API feature: client-side stream multiplexing combined with first-class tool-calling and typed/structured output primitives exposed through SDK ergonomics. Goal is to let product teams wire multiple logical consumers (UI renderers, long-running action handlers, telemetry collectors) to a single low-latency streaming connection to Redwood’s hosted endpoint, while keeping semantics for tool invocations and typed outputs clear, debuggable, and easy to adopt from client libraries.

Problem statement:
- Customers building rich UI/agents need to receive incremental tokens, structured tool calls, and metadata without opening multiple endpoints or rehydrating state.
- Current streaming surface is single linear token stream; tooling and UI teams often duplicate parsing logic, reconnect behavior, and backpressure handling in each client.
- When a large response mixes narrative text + tool calls + tabular structured output, clients struggle to reconstruct the original intent, and fallbacks (e.g., alternative model variant or offline queueing) are awkward to coordinate.

High-level goals:
- Allow multiple logical channels (render, tools, schema updates, progress events) to be multiplexed over a single websocket/HTTP/2 stream.
- Provide first-class SDK listener primitives: onSegment, onToolCall, onStructuredBlock, onCheckpoint, onError with consistent semantics across languages.
- Preserve incremental streaming semantics (partial tokens, partial tool arguments) while ensuring deterministic reassembly for structured outputs.
- Build ergonomics that minimize user parsing code; SDKs should supply canonical reconstructor utilities.
- Enable graceful fallbacks: automatic reroute to fallback model variant or non-streaming mode if latency/SLOs breached.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not define new model output formats at the model training level. We assume models emit token streams and occasional structured annotations (already supported).
- We are not shipping a new server-side runtime — implementation will map to existing streaming runtime with a framing layer and router changes.

Primary user stories:
- As a mobile engineer, I want to connect once and subscribe to "render" and "tool" channels so the UI can update progressively and run tools when invoked.
- As an SDK user, I want a simple pattern to register handlers and get a reconstructed JSON object for structured output blocks without writing my own buffer logic.
- As a platform engineer, I want predictable SLOs and metrics per logical channel to instrument cost and latency.

Success metrics (90-day):
- Adoption: 12 internal teams onboarded to multiplexed stream SDK in beta.
- Developer experience: SDK parsing error rate < 1% for structured blocks.
- Performance: average end-to-end first-byte latency on render channel <= baseline + 10ms overhead.
- Reliability: automatic fallback engages correctly in 100% of simulated capacity-surge tests.

Proposed design (conceptual):
1) Framing and channel IDs
- Server frames tokens into messages annotated with channel_id and seq_no. Minimal frame: {channel_id, frame_type, payload_fragment, seq_no, stream_epoch}.
- Channel types: render, tool_call, structured, progress, meta. Clients register interest in channel(s) at start.

2) Incremental tool-calling semantics
- Tool calls can arrive incrementally: tool_call frames contain partial arguments. SDK reassembles by seq_no and emits onToolCall when tool_call end marker observed.
- Tool lifecycle events: tool_invocation_started, tool_invocation_update, tool_invocation_completed, tool_invocation_error.

3) Structured output blocks
- Models may emit structured blocks (JSON table, jsonl records, typed schema). These are transmitted with type annotations and chunked fragments. SDK reconstructs and validates against optional schema hints supplied in the request.
- Validation failures surface via onStructuredBlock(error=...) rather than throwing uncaught exceptions.

4) Multiplexing transport choices
- Websocket: low-latency, server-push friendly.
- HTTP/2 streaming: fall back where websockets blocked.
- Long-poll / chunked HTTP as last resort.
- SDK abstracts transport; same listener API regardless of transport.

5) SDK ergonomics patterns (cross-language):
- Core API: startStream(requestOptions) -> StreamHandle
- StreamHandle.subscribe({channels: ["render","tool"], handlers: {onSegment, onToolCall, onStructuredBlock, onError, onClose}})
- Handlers receive canonical objects: Segment {text_fragment, partial, seq_no, channel_id, timestamp}, ToolCall {name, args, status, invocation_id}, StructuredBlock {schema_hint, reconstructed, validation_status}
- Utilities: reconstructStructured(schemaHint, fragments) -> validatedObject; prettyPrinter(streamHandle) -> human readable debug output.

6) Backpressure & flow control
- SDK exposes per-channel buffer limits and a backpressure callback: onBackpressure(channel_id, buffer_size). Clients can temporarily drop non-critical channels (e.g., telemetry) or ask server for lower-fidelity outputs.
- Recommend default buffer: 64KB per channel on mobile, 256KB on desktop/servers.

7) Fallbacks & routing policies
- Client may pass a routing_policy in requestOptions: prefer_latency, prefer_cost, prefer_quality. Server chooses model variant and may signal "fallback_needed" event if SLOs degrade. SDK will either auto-fallback to designated fallback variant or pause streaming and retry non-streaming completion.

API sketches (plain examples):
- Start: startStream({model: "redwood-2-mux", channels: ["render","tool","structured"], schema_hints: [{path: "order.items", type: "array"}]})
- Handler signature: onToolCall(toolCall){ if(toolCall.status=="completed") runTool(toolCall.name, toolCall.args) }

Rollout plan (phases):
- Alpha (internal only, 4 weeks): JS/TS SDK prototype, server framing toggled behind flag, 2 internal teams testing UI integration.
- Beta (partners, 8 weeks): Add Python + Java SDKs, shape backpressure defaults, integrate with Console per-route channel metrics.
- GA (quarterly): Stabilize, improve docs, provide migration guide from existing streaming API, publish performance benchmarks.

Observability and debugging:
- Emit canonical trace event when channel reassembly fails (with payload hashes, not raw PII).
- Console: per-route breakdown by channel, reconstructed structured output counts, tool invocation success/failure rates.

Open questions / risks:
- How do we ensure strong ordering guarantees across reconnection events? Proposed: stream_epoch + last_seq_no handshake causes server to replay frames from last_seq_no, but this needs storage/retention implications.
- Schema hints: how to represent optional/nullable fields without being overly verbose?
- Transport adaptation: best-effort behavior when switching from websocket to HTTP/2 mid-stream.
- Mobile resource constraints: need to measure memory/CPU impact of reassembly logic.

Next steps and action items:
- Engineering: prototype frame encoder/decoder and replay proto (Lin Wei, Diego Morales) — 2 weeks.
- SDK: JS SDK subscribe API + utilities (Ava Thompson) — 3 weeks.
- Product: finalize success metrics and acceptance criteria (Samira Patel) — 1 week.
- SRE: evaluate server-side replay retention cost (Morgan Blake) — 2 weeks.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a cross-cutting, API-first draft. Focus on the listener/handler ergonomics and the failure semantics (what does the client see when reassembly fails or when a tool call partially arrives).
- We should coordinate with Console team for new channel-level telemetry needs before beta.

Potential docs/links to add for beta:
- Migration guide: single-stream -> multiplexed stream mapping examples.
- Debugging guide: how to interpret prettyPrinter output and correlate with Console traces.
- SDK cookbook: patterns for hybrid apps (background tool handlers + foreground render subscription).

-----
End of draft.
